title: Optional & Readonly Properties
summary: Optional properties may be missing, while readonly properties should not be reassigned.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: `name?: string` means an object may have a string `name` property or may omit it. It is like an optional question on a form. Code should check that the value exists before using string methods. Use optional fields when absence has a clear meaning, rather than making every field optional for convenience. For example, a profile can omit a nickname while requiring an account ID.

subtopics.title: Important part
subtopics.explanation: Check an optional property before calling a method or using it as a definite value. For example, test `if (user.name)` when an empty name also counts as absent, or check `user.name !== undefined` when empty text is valid. It is like checking whether a form answer was filled in before reading it. For example, check `name !== undefined` when an empty string is still a valid value.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: `readonly id: string` prevents code using that type from assigning a new value to `id`. It is like printing an ID on a badge that should not be edited. This is a compile-time rule. Other code or JavaScript can still change the object unless runtime protections are added. For example, mark a creation timestamp readonly when callers should not replace it.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: Readonly is shallow unless applied to nested property types as well. A readonly property that points to an object does not automatically freeze the object inside. It is like protecting a folder label while leaving its papers editable. Use immutable data patterns or runtime freezing when the application needs deeper protection. For example, a readonly object property can still point to a mutable nested array.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: Use an optional field only when the data model permits it to be missing. Use readonly when callers should treat a value as stable. These types document expectations for developers, much like labels on a shared form. TypeScript checks those expectations during development, but the program still needs validation for data arriving from outside. For example, validate optional server fields before rendering controls that depend on them.

foundations.overview: TypeScript properties can be optional or marked readonly. An optional property may be absent; a readonly property cannot be reassigned through that type. Think of an optional field as a form question someone may skip, and a readonly ID as a printed label. These checks improve code safety, but `readonly` does not freeze data at runtime or make nested objects immutable.
foundations.whyItMatters: Optional and readonly modifiers make data contracts more precise. They help developers understand absence and reassignment rules without pretending to provide runtime validation.
foundations.browserPerspective: Both modifiers are erased at compile time. At runtime the object is an ordinary, fully mutable JavaScript object — readonly is not Object.freeze. For runtime immutability you must freeze explicitly.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Optional props (title?: string), readonly ids and config, Readonly<Props> in components, and readonly arrays for data you only iterate are everyday uses.
foundations.businessImpact: Marking fields readonly prevents a class of mutation bugs (shared state changed unexpectedly) that are hard to trace in production, reducing incident time and risk.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Modifiers make data contracts explicit, so engineers know at a glance which fields are stable and which may be missing — fewer defensive checks, safer refactors.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime cost (erased). Choosing readonly types can even help engines and reviewers reason about code, but the immutability itself is compile-time only.
commonUseCases: Optional component props and config fields
readonly ids and other set-once values
Readonly<T> for parameters you promise not to mutate
readonly arrays for collections you only read

commonMisconceptions.myth: readonly makes the object immutable at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: readonly is compile-time only; the runtime object is still mutable. Use Object.freeze for real runtime immutability.

commonMisconceptions.myth: x?: T and x: T | undefined are the same.
commonMisconceptions.reality: ? allows the property to be absent; the union requires the property to be present (possibly holding undefined). Under exactOptionalPropertyTypes they differ further.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Optional means the property may be null and undefined in every configuration.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The question mark permits absence; null must be included separately when it is a valid value.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Readonly prevents every possible mutation at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Readonly is a TypeScript checking rule and is shallow unless nested types add their own constraints.

visualExplorer.caption: Walk through how the compiler treats an optional field and rejects a readonly reassignment.

config.intro: Trace a type with { readonly id: number; nickname?: string } as you read and write its fields.

steps.name: Declare modifiers
steps.detail: interface User { readonly id: number; nickname?: string } marks id as set-once and nickname as possibly-absent.

steps.name: Construct the object
steps.detail: const u: User = { id: 1 } is valid — nickname may be omitted, id is provided.

steps.name: Read the optional field
steps.detail: u.nickname has type string | undefined, so TypeScript requires a guard before using it.

steps.name: Attempt a readonly write
steps.detail: u.id = 2 is a compile error: id is readonly and can't be reassigned.

steps.name: Remember runtime reality
steps.detail: All checks are erased; at runtime the object is mutable JS — readonly is a promise to the compiler only.

codeLab.title: Lock down a config shape
codeLab.instructions: Type the Settings so theme is required and readonly, fontSize is optional, and the function parameter cannot be mutated. Use readonly and ?.
hints: Add readonly before theme and a ? after fontSize.
Wrap the parameter type in Readonly<Settings> to forbid mutation.

keyTakeaways: `name?: string` means an object may have a string `name` property or may omit it.
Check an optional property before calling a method or using it as a definite value.
`readonly id: string` prevents code using that type from assigning a new value to `id`.
Readonly is shallow unless applied to nested property types as well.
Use an optional field only when the data model permits it to be missing.
